utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everybody. Good afternoon, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Excellency. Good afternoon to all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon. I hope that you will understand that the documents that pertain to the period of your command in Bosnia, as well as your book, and my correspondence with your political chief, Mr. Akashi, and your correspondence with Mladic and other officers of ours, is of key importance for understanding the entire situation as it was. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You had rather fair and critical assessments of the Western governments, in view of understanding the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina; right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I felt that the Western governments had a confused strategy with regards to the resolution of the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina during my period in command there in 1994, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we call up page 3 of the book, General Rose's book, that is, 1D1037. Page 3 of the book, rather.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, I note that General Rose has just reached for his paperback version of his book, which I noticed yesterday isn't the same version as we have in e-court. And I wonder, subject with Your Honours' leave and, of course, Dr. Karadzic's, if we might be able to provide him with a copy that, in fact, is the scanned copy that appears in e-court, and that way he would be able to find the pages more easily himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That would be very helpful. Thank you, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If the usher could pass the book along to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And there is -- of course, the only marking in that is the name which appears inside the front cover, which is my own, which is the same as what appears in e-court.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think that the Defence would mind that. In the meantime, can you --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we have it now in e-court.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we take a brief look at a paragraph on page number 3, where you said that the Western coalition, led by America, was deluded in believing that Bosnia is like Iraq, and you said that it wasn't all that simple because, quite simply, it wasn't that one country invaded another country. We have to find -- [In English] "... pointed out that the international coalition led by America took military --" [Interpretation] Towards the bottom. We can't see that paragraph yet. Could you scroll down a bit more. We see the first sentence only: "Bosnians frequently pointed out ...," et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So this is your observation and your position; isn't that right? It's that first paragraph down there.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found the paragraph. And your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that what I said, that that was an observation of yours, that there was a lack of understanding among Western governments, in terms of the nature of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Excellencies, later on I would like to tender these pages, once we are done with all of them. So it's this paragraph, starting with: "Bosnians frequently ..." et cetera, going all the way down to: "... Croatia and Serbia." Could we now have page 59.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that Western diplomats, primarily American diplomats, came with some prejudice or with some tasks that were dissonant from the situation on the ground, and that that constituted a problem for you as well?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to any specific paragraph on page 59?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, once I see it -- [In English] "... Ambassador Charles Redman, President Clinton's special envoy."

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I find the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's this paragraph: "Not to be outdone ..." And then further on, it says, "Bosnian Serbs," et cetera, "congressional elections." I would like to indicate this sentence: "I explained --" [In English] "... to be more than happy to stop the fighting while they are ahead, and that it had been the Muslims who had tried to renege from the meeting at the airport." [Interpretation] Further on, you say that Redman repeated that the Serbs should not be allowed to benefit from their aggression and that nothing would stop America from establishing a unitary Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that actually you -- your understanding was that Western diplomats came there with a ready-made agenda, regardless of what was happening on the ground; right?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, before there's an answer, what was translated from what Dr. Karadzic said was not quite what the paragraph on the screen reads from the book. And, of course, it was a compound question.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The interpretation was exactly what Dr. Karadzic said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So we have the paragraph of the book in front of us. Mr. Karadzic, what is your question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question for General Rose, who had observed this, is -- is whether they came there with an agenda that was not made on the basis of the situation on the ground but, rather, on the basis of their own internal political needs, as you had observed in this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My reply is their agenda, when I spoke to Mr. Redman, as I understood it, was different from that of the United Nations Protection Force at the time, certainly in terms of the priorities that were established by the United Nations. Their goal was a just solution and a just peace, whereas the United Nations' first priority was the continued delivery of humanitarian aid, and only second to that would have been the pursuit of a just peace. It was a question of priority, not necessarily a different agenda.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you do recall that the Christian majority, consisting of the Serbs and Croats, did not accept a unitary Bosnia-Herzegovina, right, and that the creation of a unitary Bosnia-Herzegovina would not have been a just solution? And it hasn't worked to this day. Also, this was the main cause of the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I counted three questions and a statement in there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: However, I let it go because I believe the general could -- would be able to deal with this question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a great debate at the time partly between the United Nations and the warring parties. It continued with the contact group and other interested parties about how best to bring about a peaceful resolution of the problem, and most of the suggested solutions certainly involved a redistribution of the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina amongst the warring parties. But that re-division of territory generally was supposedly a temporary arrangement, not a permanent one. People still had the goal that Bosnia should ultimately return to its unitary state, I think. But I was a military man on the ground, with a limited knowledge of the political debates that were going on around me and above me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, as Ms. Edgerton advised you, you would be better off if you would make your question one by one, more simple and direct. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then I'm going to move on from political questions and get closer to issues related to peace and humanitarian issues. Was your position and was it your observation that the full demilitarisation of Sarajevo -- and we have already established that for the Bosnians and Muslims, that was a problem for several reasons, because they would have to leave Sarajevo -- I mean, their army would have to leave it, and ours would have to leave it, too, but the problem was that the financial gains from the control of movement would have gone down. So from that point of view, was your conclusion that the extremists and the SDA believed that it would be better to have shells and bombs fall rather than to demilitarise Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of any financial gains or losses that could be made by either side, and certainly I discussed with many parties and none of them said to me that it would be better to continue having shells fall on Sarajevo rather than demilitarise. That was never said to me by anybody.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have page 45 of the book. 45 of the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May I draw your attention to this paragraph: "Full demilitarisation of Sarajevo ..." [In English] "... for the Bosnians or all Bosnian army units. For the Bosnian Government, this was a step too far, and as it would mean that they were no longer sovereign in their own capital. Handing over the security of Sarajevo to the UN would also reduce the possibility of any financial gains that control of all movements in and out of the city generated for the party leaders. In the view of some extremists of the SDS [sic], it was better to keep the shells falling on their own people, in the hope that the US would one day enter the war on their own side and to conceal this inhumane strategy; they continued to blame the world for allowing slow-motion genocide to take place in their country."

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: My words written in that paragraph were written two or three years after I'd left Bosnia and were a post facto assessment I had made. I repeat, no one during my time in Bosnia ever mentioned financial gain or loss to me, or, indeed, advocated the continual shelling of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The transcript may be saying "SDS," but it is actually the SDA extremists and party leaders who were -- I mean, who had an interest in not establishing peace.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you have any knowledge to that effect; namely, that Ganic and other extremists were not in favour of peace?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I explained yesterday, it was not in the strategic interests of the Bosnian Government at that time in 1994 to bring about a cessation of hostilities which might result in a permanent peace; a Cyprus-isation as they called it, of the situation, which would end up having an unfair division of territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, with all due respect, the first part of your knowledge, as it were, is quite understandable for me, but the second part is an interpretation, as if that would be the case, et cetera. But don't you see that at the conference we practically lost all of the Serb Sarajevo and the territorial questions could not have been resolved by military means but only at the conference, and that perhaps there was another reason involved; namely, why they didn't want to have the war brought to an end?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of the debate that occurred at the Dayton Conference, which is presumably the conference you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But do you recall that it was clear, invariably, that there would be a political assessment found at a conference, not a military solution? We held all of the surrounding area of Sarajevo, and we lost all of it, but at the green table, not in the battle-field, so we have to look at other reasons why Muslims -- or at least Muslim extremists in the Presidency did not want peace. That is why I'm drawing your attention to this, to see whether there were other reasons, too, not this one. This one clearly cannot be accepted, because it was obvious that a fait accompli would not be accepted.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot make any comment of any value at all to this Court about subjects which occurred outside my period of command in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I was just referring to two parts of the position you expressed. The first part is that you say that they didn't want to, and the second part is why. I mean, that doesn't seem convincing to me, and we have evidence to the effect that things were different. However, you have clearly seen for yourself hundreds of times -- or I don't know how many times, but you have seen the Muslim side firing at the UN, and at NATO aircraft, and at their own people, and at the Serb side, in order to cause a Serb response and to create an image of constant warfare and constant suffering; right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not say hundreds of times. The occasions which we suspected this was happening were very few, indeed, in terms of evidence that was produced mainly, of course, by Sector Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you will agree that even the best crime police in the world catches only 5 or 10 per cent of all perpetrators and the rest just get away. What I would like to present to the Trial Chamber is the pattern that we had to deal with. So now I would like to ask for page -- well, actually, let us have a look at this, what you talked about just now, page 197 and 198, where you presented a perfectly clear view that firing at one's own civilians in order to provoke Serb fire is practically one and the same thing; right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which paragraph are you referring to, Dr. Karadzic, on that page 197?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [In English] "More serious were reports we started to receive from the French in the city that the Bosnian forces were sometimes firing on their own citizens. In one such incident, a tram had been fired on from a building of the Bosnian side of the conflict line, normally occupied by paramilitary police. In another incident following a mortar attack near the Presidency that killed two children, two more shells had been fired at the same location while a French Army team was investigating the first incident. This secondary shot should [sic] only have come from the Bosnian side of the firing line. On the other side of the city, on several occasions, UN and NATO aircraft at Sarajevo Airport had been fired at from the Muslim-held suburb of Butmir."

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was certainly my view at the time, this is what had occurred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The transcript should read "the secondary shots could only have come from" instead of "should only have come from." Continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: "Could only have." [Interpretation] "Could only have."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's just finish with this part, the other part: "The Bosnian Government," and then we'll go back -- let's look at all of it. [In English] "Nevertheless, in my view, the moral distinction between Bosnian forces firing at the Serbs, with the intention to provoke retaliation against civilians, and the Bosnians themselves firing on their own people, is a fine one." [Interpretation] So that is your position, and that is what I meant a few moments ago.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is my position.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We share that position. Now, do you know that often the tram was fired at in order to have the Serb side accused, and that these were not only allegations, there was clear evidence provided for that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your -- whenever we protested about the firing on the trams, the reply from the Bosnian Serb side always was that it was done by the Bosnian Government forces in order to discredit the Bosnian Serb side. I think there was one occasion, and in many instances this happened, where evidence was produced by the French Sector, showing that this may, indeed, have been the case. One incident.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have 1D2945. We'll go back to the book later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the incident that you referred to, the incident when the French caught the perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to a paragraph in the book, Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that there were incidents when the tram was shot at from the Muslim side. Do you remember when that particular incident occurred, the one that was investigated by the French?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: You'll have to give me a reference in the either book or the witness statement I made that you have a copy of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: He seems to be calling up a document, 1D2945. Is that the document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure about the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But, anyway, General, while the book is still here, have a look at this; that there was firing -- [In English] "... such incident. A tram had been fired on from a building on the Bosnian side of the conflict line normally occupied by paramilitary police." [Interpretation] Do you remember when that particular incident with the tram occurred?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could you go back to page 197 and the image that's on the screen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The paragraph we saw earlier on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think we need to cross-reference - it would be a witness statement that I made - in order to identify the date.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You are aware of at least one such incident. You are aware of the pattern or the phenomenon: [In English] "... a tram had been fired from the building on the Bosnian side." [Interpretation] What I would like to know now is whether you know when this particular incident had occurred, the incident regarding which you had received information from the French stating that Muslim perpetrators had been caught.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's quite clear I can't remember the date. I'm looking for it in the witness statement. It was over 15 years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I wasn't dealing with the statement. I was dealing with the book. But let us look at 1D2485. Could we have that in e-court, please. Yes, that's the document, an UNPROFOR document from the 27th of October, 1994. Right? Do you agree that this is an assessment regarding problems concerning the airport, Civilian Affairs, and the importance of Igman? If you remember, we had been forced to leave Igman because of this ultimatum of NATO.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Could you scroll down the document so we can see the whole document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first page. We're actually interested in the second page. I just wanted General Rose to confirm that it says: "The importance of Igman is well known ... [In English] "... and they may not agree on the shooting of this."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You do recall, don't you, that Muslims were partly on Igman and we partly handed over to you, the UN, or, rather, General Briquemont, the part that we had held? The Muslims were still firing at us, but we were prevented from firing at Igman. Remember that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The NATO ultimatum required the Serb forces to move off Mount Igman, and the Muslim forces, the Bosnian Government forces, not to advance from where their positions were. And that was the position I inherited in 1994; that is so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can you answer the question, General, regarding the Muslims were still firing at them and they were prevented from firing at Igman?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What happened on Mount Igman was that the Bosnian Government forces started to launch attacks across Mount Igman, through the demilitarised zone, at the Serb positions on the other side of the demilitarised zone, and NATO, who was responsible for enforcing the demilitarised of that area -- the demilitarisation of that area, had failed to take action against the Bosnian Government forces. In spite of the fact we had protested to the Bosnian Government that they should cease doing this, they continued to do so. When we asked NATO to take action against them whenever they did make incursions, NATO refused to do so. That is the case.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we please go to the next page of the document, page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We can see here "1735 hours, 25th October." It is probably "Fraternity and Unity Bridge," and reported eight injured. [In English] "... investigation, see report conclusion." [Interpretation] And then the last bullet in the conclusions: [In English] "All evidence and corroboration by Bosnian officials indicate shots came from Bosnian-held territory." [Interpretation] Was that the incident that you were referring to or was that a totally different incident?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Without any particular knowledge of whether it was that incident, I suspect it was.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like to tender the document into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see the document notes "map should be attached," the paragraph in bold on the page in front of us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Which is missing. With that noting, we'll admit this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D681, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Since we are talking about this, General, do you remember that Ejub Ganic had organised secret police that snipe the trams in Sarajevo, and all those incidents were supposed to be assigned to the Serbian side; the Serbs were to be blamed for all those?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I explained before, we had no intelligence-gathering capability, so I wouldn't be -- have been at the time able to confirm or deny such an allegation, and I certainly can't do so today.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now draw the participants' attention to the information report, [In English] 28th of August, 2003. [Interpretation] 1D2475, can we have this brought up in e-court. Could we please see page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You see you are not pro-Serbian, General, sir. You say here: "But it must be a different thing." Number 3 in the document, you say here: [In English] "I'm sure that the Serbs were firing at the tram, but I believe Ganic also organised his secret police to snipe tram. His sniper units sniped so that the angle of the shot matched the direction from the Serb line. During the long cease-fire, I think that Ganic and the Muslims were responsible for breaking the cease-fire. This kept the tensions ...," and so on. [Interpretation] How could you be so sure about the Serbs and you believed about Ganic? Wouldn't we have been complete imbeciles if we had fired in front of Holiday Inn, in view of everybody who was there; the journalists, the observers, and everybody else?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I say, we had no intelligence-gathering capability, and so I would -- although there were suspicions that that was happening at the time and there was some evidence which we referred to, I can make no further comment than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you agree with me that as soon as something like that happened, that would have called for a complete and thorough investigation; right? And you did not have any capabilities to investigate; therefore, you didn't investigate, did you?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're referring to Sector Sarajevo and the French Command, they investigated every incident, as, indeed, did the United Nations Military Observers. I got the reports from Sector Sarajevo as to what might or might not have happened on the ground; I did not get the reports from the United Nations Military Observers.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: General, you can confirm what is stated in this information sheet; i.e., that you believe Ganic organised his secret police to snipe trams?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was certainly our belief at the time, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And can we now look at pages 79 and 80 in the book. Since we're talking about Ganic, let's shed some more light on his significance. 79 and 80 in the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your view, was Ganic rather extreme and a major hindrance when it came to establishing peace?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was often the case, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we scroll down, where it says: "In Washington ...," so everybody can read and see that Silajdzic had agreed that the airport in Tuzla should be reopened, but Ganic went back on the agreement and demanded that the Fraternity and Unity Bridge could be reopened, and then from there we have to go to the following page, where it says: "On the other hand --" [In English] "Ganic, on the other hand, who was responsible for the Bosnian armed forces and the paramilitary police, had become even more powerful. He remained close to President Izetbegovic, and by the end of 1994 he was the main point of contact between the UN and the Bosnian Government. As a member of the inner cabinet, he also controlled the Bosnian press, radio and television."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, General, sir, that we accepted that the airport in Tuzla should be opened on the condition that we had at least one officer there who will monitor the situation and see whether weapons were being off-loaded there?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that being the situation very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you remember that the Muslim side persisted on not allowing any control of any of the transports at that airport?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: If by "control," you mean inspection, that is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Precisely. We just wanted to see or observe or just be able to tell whether weapons were being off-loaded there, that's all. Do you remember that that was not allowed, that we were not even allowed to inspect, the Serbs were not even allowed to inspect?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That they were not allowed to station an inspectorate at Tuzla Airport in the case that the UN could fly a direct at Tuzla, that is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you hear or see or learn that the airport at Tuzla was the place where a lot of weapons entered Bosnia from Iran and other countries?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only transports into Tuzla during my time in 1994 were UN humanitarian aid transports, and they certainly didn't contain any weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well, General, sir. We will show documents - maybe not during your cross-examination - that there were night flights and landing of unidentified aircraft that brought weapons in, but we will leave that until later. General, sir, immediately after your arrival, a major incident took place at the Markale Market; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at page 48 in the book, in your book. We just want to look at one paragraph, and we will move on to other documents after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the page to be displayed: Did you read "Balkan Odyssey" by Lord Owen?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I draw your attention to the paragraph starting with the following words: "... had now agreed virtually everything ..." [Interpretation] Scroll down, scroll down to the bottom of the page. Thank you. I don't want to read. I would like the participants to notice that the gist of the passage is that the Serbs, after that incident, accepted everything that had been requested by the Bosnian Government, but the Bosnian Government still was not willing to sign a peace agreement and accept the UN proposals. In any case, the UN proposals were not dealing with a long-term solution, and they were very angry about the strategy of -- was not successful. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you may have to be more precise in your question, Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, you can read, all of the Serb -- [In English] "... had now agreed virtually everything the Bosnians had asked for, Divjak was reluctant to sign up to a cease-fire, once again on the grounds that the UN proposal was not linked to any long-term political settlement. I told him that the people of Sarajevo would at that moment certainly settle for something short of this, just to be able to live in peace. He still would not agree. At this point, I sprang a nasty surprise on him. I told him that the first UN examination of the bomb crater in the Markale marketplace indicated the bomb had been fired from the Bosnian side of the battle lines. The room went deadly silent and Hajrulahovic looked anxious. He coldly asked me to explain. I told him that the angle of the trajectory of the mortar bomb suggested that it had been fired at extremely short range from their side of the lines or perhaps detonated in-situ. It was difficult, I said, to be precise when only one bomb had been fired and also because the Bosnian Army had removed some of the important forensic evidence before the UN arrived."

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: And your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question is this -- the first one is this: After the incidents, did the Serbs mostly accept all Muslim proposals, but they, on the other hand, still did not agree to sign up to a cease-fire? That's what you write in this passage.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you know, at the meeting at the airport the next day, an agreement was reached between Ganic -- between Delic and Mladic that there should be a cease-fire, leading to a withdrawal of heavy weapons from around Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I agree that you managed to mediate in that cease-fire, but it says here that at first they didn't accept that. My second question is this: Is it correct that they changed the position where the bomb had been detonated and that they had presented a certain forensic evidence in order to further aggravate the work of the investigators who wanted to establish the responsibility for the incident?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's impossible to answer that question in -- without putting it into context. What happened was the initial inspection was as described in the paragraph you have read out, that a subsequent inspection changed the view and made it more likely that the bomb had been fired from the Serb side. So the initial, immediate inspection was as in the paragraph, that it was likely to have been fired from the Bosnian side, which is why I made the point to the Bosnian Government people, but the subsequent examination showed another possibility, that it had come, i.e., from the Bosnian Serb side. But, of course, as I explained previously, crater analysis is a very inexact science.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. However, in your view, what was the best moment, or in general terms, what is the best moment to investigate an incident and provide an expert report? Would it be best to do it immediately after the incident or some time later?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, assuming the technical advice was available immediately after the incident, that, surely, would be the best time to conduct a forensic examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. 65 ter 06285 is the next document, and then page 116 [as interpreted] in e-court. This is Lord Owen's book, "The Balkan Odyssey." Page 160 is the page I would like to be brought up in e-court. That was not properly recorded the first time 'round.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that any intervention at the place of the incident unables [as interpreted] or at least makes any forensic examination more difficult? It seems I was wrong. The document in e-court is page 160. That's the e-court page. And in the book, itself, the page number is 279. In other words, General, sir, is it allowed to change the place of an incident and then undertake a new forensic examination?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if evidence has been interfered with on the ground, then, of course, the subsequent investigation may be less than perfect. But I think you're referring to the removal of a tail-fin which identified the type of mortar that had been fired, and, of course, the removal of the tail-fin doesn't necessarily change the shape of the crater. And it was crater analysis that was being examined as a part of the procedure, not necessarily just identifying the form of weapon that had been used. But there were two investigations, one an immediate one by French engineers, and then subsequently by a technical team that came from elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And that team came from where? The second team, whose team was that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It came from the UN.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. We'll see later -- or, rather, first we will see how important it is where the tail was, and we'll see that the crater had been changed. May I draw your attention to this passage: "On Tuesday, 8 February ..." [In English] "... querying the UN objection to demilitarisation and arguing for an exclusion zone smaller than the 30-kilometre radius advocated by the French and accompanied by the confidence-building measures. The Bosnian Government delegation which was due to negotiate did not, however, turn up at the Sarajevo Airport for the negotiating session that morning. General Rose was reportedly furious and went to the Bosnian Presidency to persuade President Izetbegovic and his military chief, General Delic, to attend." [Interpretation] Is this true, what is written in here?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I guess Lord Owen was using that paragraph in my book that we've already referred to, and to that extent, yes, it was true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And further on, it says: [In English] "And now General Rose had never made a secret of the fact that at that meeting he told the Bosnian Muslim leaders that he had just received technical information which pointed to the mortar bomb having come not from Serb-controlled areas but from a Muslim-controlled area. If this information were made available, there would be a very different outcome of the NATO meeting, and if Izetbegovic tried to stall the UN negotiations ..." [Interpretation] Can we have the following page: [In English] "... in order to wait for the NATO meeting, he, Rose, would feel obliged to release the preliminary evidence of the UN investigation." [Interpretation] Do you agree that the Muslim side was afraid at what you had found out?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I say, the preliminary investigation was followed by a more detailed subsequent investigation with a higher technical level of competence, and the position of the United Nations changed from the immediate thought that it could have come from the Bosnian Government side to it having more likely come from the Bosnian Serb side. I also said at the time, to the media, that given the four mortar bombs that had been fired a day or two before at the UN aid queue in Dobrinja, which had definitely come from the Serb side, then it was most likely that the market-place bomb had also come from the Serb side, but people would have to draw their own conclusions about that. I made that statement to the press prior to the second UN investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We will be dealing with another investigation, too, but let us see what Lord Owen says: [In English] "... would have been more circumspect about what happened at this meeting, but I know that he had sent, on Tuesday, a report that said the mortar shell might have been launched by the Bosnian Army side and that they were continuing their investigation. In addition, a senior ballistics expert in Zagreb had studied a map of likely trajectory patterns produced by UN investigators in Sarajevo and believed the angle at which the mortar had hit the roof of the market stall indicated that the firing point was more likely to be 1.100 to 2.000 metres from the impact than 2.000 to 3.000 metres, and that this would tend to indicate that the mortar had been fired from a Bosnian Army position. When this highly-charged information reached the UN in New York on Tuesday, everything was done to clamp down on the number of people who saw it so as to reduce the chance of a press leak." [Interpretation] So, General, there were a great many of them who were involved in this clamp-down on the possible leak regarding this first on-site investigation just so that the Serbs would remain accused; right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to -- I'm not in a position, Dr. Karadzic, to say more than I've already said, and that is that Lord Owen referred, in the paragraph you just read out, to the report I sent based on the initial French engineers' report. What happened subsequently to that report and other comments that may have been made, either in Zagreb or New York, is something that you'll have to ask Dr. Owen, or Lord Owen as he is now, if he attends this Court. I can't make any comment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page. I mean, it's the same page, but just the other half, as it were, of this page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, the first findings had -- the first findings stated that in all likelihood it was the Serb side that had fired. That would have been made public straight away. Why was that not done in this case, when the Muslim side was initially blamed?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you just repeat that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that invariably, in similar situations, when there was even the slimmest of chances that the Serbs had done something, that was made public immediately, whereas in this case the first investigation had established that it was done by the Muslims? Why was that concealed from the media?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think any effort was made by the United Nations to conceal any of the reports at my level. If attempts were made elsewhere, I have no knowledge of that. Certainly, after every incident, an examination was made, and press queries were answered to the best of our ability. We were, after all, peacekeepers working with parties to try and bring about a peace. We were not parties to that conflict, ourselves, and had no secrets to hide, therefore.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid that from time to time, you were a warring party as well, but we'll get to that. But look at what Lord Owen says. He said in dramatic terms everything was done in New York in order to have the smallest number of persons know about this so it would not be leaked to the media. Lord Owen should be trusted, and I fully trust him at this point in time; namely, that everything possible was done in order to prevent this from leaking out. How do you explain that, that it was not leaked out immediately? Why did one have to dig in order to get that report?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Questioned and answered. Move on to your next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's have a look at this on this page. Can you see on this page that the Serbs were in favour of an investigation, and then Lord Owen says. [In English] "If we knew that the Bosnian Serbs got a negative response in establishing an inquiry, the Geneva talks would collapse. Our dilemma was acute, for if the slightest hint that the Muslims were thought to be responsible came out of the ICFY in Geneva, the Bosnian Muslims would not attend. NATO, having just taken its decision, would also be in disarray if the public perception of the Serbs being responsible for the market-place bomb were suddenly shattered. What was needed was a little news management of the sort that international organisations are not very good at; above all, the United Nations in New York had to come under pressure from the press to establish the facts -- and I arranged quietly that this was done. I did not feel it was right for me to do anything more than this. I was in receipt of privileged information from the UN. I could not allow a cover-up, but equally it was not for me to break the story." [Interpretation] General, do you agree that ruses of war are a customary thing, ascribing something to the enemy?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, as I've said before, with regards to Lord Owen's book, I can only comment on my personal dealings with him and the reports that I may have made that he was in receipt of. I cannot comment on anything else with any value.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But my question was whether ruses of war are customary; namely, that one side does something in order to blacken the other side, as it were. Does something like that happen in war? All is fair in love and war, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, propaganda certainly is in war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, it's time to have a break now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can that propaganda turn up before a court of law, General? Can that kind of propaganda aspire to be the truth, and before the highest international court of law, at that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, that's just a speculative statement that the witness can't possibly answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll break for 25 minutes and resume at 4.00. General, I forgot to mention to you yesterday, but you must be well aware of it, that during the break or the adjournment, you are not supposed to discuss your evidence with anybody else.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now I would like to tender those pages from Lord Owen's book, page 279 from the book, and 280 and 281, the ones that we quoted from here. Could that be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you would like to tender only those three pages?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: It is already an exhibit, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think we admitted one or two pages so far. And you are -- you went through a lot of pages, but you are tendering -- my question is whether you are minded to tender only those three pages referred to; i.e., page 279 to 281?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Lest I create any confusion, I'm talking about Lord Owen's book, not Sir Michael's book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was confused, yes. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it's from Lord Owen's book that I'm tendering these three pages, 279, 280, and 281, along with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I note that the general couldn't confirm some parts of it. But I'd like to ask Ms. Edgerton as to your position.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I only note that, as far as what I can see on the screen and what I'm able to review on the transcript, we never saw page 281 nor did we discuss page 281. It's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We read some part of 281.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The right bottom part.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, and my apologies.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: No objection?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, no objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that part will be added to the exhibit which was already admitted. Can I be reminded of the exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That was Exhibit P799.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Just to be easier to everyone. [Interpretation] Lord Owen says what happened in New York on the basis of General Rose's report, so, indeed, we should be happy that this has been admitted. Can we now have 65 ter 9630.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, the United Nations dealt with Markale far more in depth than you had been aware of. We're now calling up that UN document. It's the first page, actually. Can we now have page 19 in e-court. The entire document is actually an analysis by Captain Verdy and other participants on behalf of the UN. It's an analysis of what had happened at Markale.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's actually P1441, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. It was noted in his list as well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I now have page 19 in e-court. Yes, that's the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, General, let us have a look at this. I would actually like to recommend this paragraph A, "Estimate," to all. Let's look at the next one, though: "By the time ..." [In English] "... the team conducted its analysis, six days had elapsed since the explosion. It is reasonable to suspect that the crater was totally excavated by the local authorities during that period. Hence, the angles measured on 11th of February are not beyond suspicion." [Interpretation] So they were rigging this, the crater. The local authorities were rigging the crater in order to direct all suspicions against the Serbs. These UN findings say that this subsequent measuring is the one that's suspicious, not the first one. Is that what it says here, General?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you answer: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It was a request for a clarification that may already be there in Dr. Karadzic's question, whether or not this page that's currently displayed refers to the first analysis conducted or the second analysis conducted and in what regard Captain Verdy was involved.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is clear here that the investigator is referring to the investigation carried out on the 11th, that is to say, five days after the explosion. In the meantime, it's not only that the site -- the point of impact had deteriorated in its own right, but it had been tampered with by the local authorities. Now, this second analysis is the one that is being brought into question by this UN investigator, not the first one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Right, General?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I say, no, I'm not in a position to make any comment on this report. I'm not a technician, I was not involved in the writing of this report; therefore, I can make no valuable comment on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But, General, on the basis of what did you trust the second findings? You stated your views on that here, not the first findings. When your own services, those of the UN, state that it is the second round of findings that is suspicious, don't you agree with that? It says here that it had been tampered with, excavated; that is to say, that they had been doing some digging there in the meantime, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: My comment is that the wording actually is: "It is reasonable to suspect that the crater was thoroughly excavated by the local authorities during that period." I've got no means of knowing whether that suspicion is right or wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then your own assertion does not stand, that the second investigation was more thorough and that it concluded that it was the Serbs that were the culprits; right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The second investigation certainly replaced the first investigation, in terms of its findings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, the second investigation -- this is the second investigation, and this is a Prosecution exhibit. And that second exhibit asserted that the place had been tampered with and it is reasonable to suspect the angle that would be determined on the basis of the alterations that had been made to the crater.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can remember at the time is that I went along with the second investigation, and it confirmed very much the public statement that I already made, which compared the shelling of the UN aid queue in Dobrinja with the shelling in the market-place. And I allowed people to draw their own conclusions, but I said that my suspicion was it had been done by the Serb side. The second investigation tended to confirm that view. Now, whether you think the second investigation was flawed or not is up to you. I made no assessment at the time of that nature. I accepted the official version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, this is precisely what I meant to ask you. Why did you correct your initial position, which was that that had been done by the Muslims, and you communicated that to Muslim officers? Why did you say not only that it was not certain who had done it, but also that it was most probable that it had been done by the Serbs? What made you change your opinion? Was it the second investigation?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd already made the assertion before the second investigation that because the Serbs had undoubtedly done the shelling in the market-place two days -- the shelling in the -- against the bread queue two days before in Dobrinja, it was most likely that Serbs had done the shelling in the market-place, since technical analysis was unable to say. The second investigation confirmed that position that I had originally taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How far is Dobrinja from Markale, General?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: You, sir, would know better than I, but I would think two miles.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would say 10 miles, or 15 kilometres, General. And if we used the analogy and if we say that the Serbs had shot from there - and they didn't, we'll establish that - how can we determine that one or two days before, they fired one shot and managed to hit Markale? What was it that made you change your opinion even before the second investigation?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: This first investigation was indeterminate. The second one was much clearer. As I said, because the first one was indeterminate, and it was stated to me that it was indeterminate, I took the position that because there had been a shelling of the bread queue, the UN aid queue in Dobrinja, it was most likely the Serbs had done the second shelling in Markale. This was confirmed, as I say, by the second report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We will see that that was not the case, General. It was just the contrary. The first conclusion was that it was the Muslims who had fired, and the second was indeterminate, that it could not be established, and I'm holding the second conclusion right in front of me. Can we now see page 36 in e-court. According to our information, there are as many as eight investigations. The first had established that it was the Muslims, and that was sent to the United Nations. Lord Owen testified that there was a great deal of concern about possible leaks to the media. And the investigation that was undertaken on the 11th of February, that was carried out by the United Nations team. A lot of people, experts, concluded that it was inclusive. So the first one ascribed the event to the Muslims, the second was inclusive. In any case, it was exculpatory for the Serbs. However, you, as a pro-Serbian officer -- a pro-Serbian officer, are unwilling to accept that. We see that it was quite unjustified when you were accused of being pro-Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I've explained, I was part of the United Nations Protection Force that was impartial in our dealings with the warring parties, although, of course, we were not exactly neutral in terms of our wish for a just and peaceful solution to the conflict. I can add no more than I've said on the subject of the Markale bombing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And we will show, General, that the Serbs considered you quite anti-Serb and that your today's testimony confirms that. I didn't want to say that, but many Serbs were of that opinion. Can we now see page 17, and let's see the number of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Your question is just unhelpful at all. Whether pro-Serb, anti-Serb, it's nothing to do with this case. Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I was rising with an objection with respect to that comment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: I think you were about to observe that it was a comment and not a question, in any event, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Quite so, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to put my question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If you had been either pro-Serb or anti-Serb, if you were either anti-Serb or pro-Serb, would that have any impact on your testimony today? Would you still be objective in providing your answers today?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already sworn to tell the truth and the whole truth, nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well, Sir Michael. I know you have been knighted and you are a decorated officer. Let's stick to that. Let's now see page 17, and let's hope that your knight's honour will compel you to tell the truth. General, sir, here you have a list of all the investigations which were carried out by a French team on the 5th February, then Captain Verdy on the 5th of February, Major Russell on the 5th of February, Major Khan on the 11th of February. Look at the list --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just to be fair to the witness and everyone, I'd like to make it clear that this page represents one of the annexes to the second investigation, or a page extracted from one of the annexes to the second investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, do you see this list containing as many as 10 different investigations?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see exactly what you see, Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that none of them established beyond a reasonable doubt that the shell came from the Serbian side, that it was not established even with a certain degree of reasonable doubt?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I say, crater analysis is an inexact science, particularly when it relates to only [Realtime transcript read in error "any"] one crater. "To only one crater," that should read.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What method could be used in order to establish who fired? Let's not talk about any scientific methods. Just tell us: Which method could be used in order to determine the culprit for the firing of that shell?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only 100 per cent accurate way of identifying the firing point of a single mortar bomb would be from mortar radar, which we didn't have at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we look at page 41 in the same document. This is in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can I draw your attention to bullet points 4 and 5. In bullet point 4, it says: [In English] "The Bosnian Serbs are close to the directional bracket is controlled by Kosevo Brigade. FreBat 4 MIO confirms the existence of a 120-millimetre mortar position at GR BP 922642, which is outside the directional bracket. Colonel Cvjetkovic, BSA Artillery Regiment commander, stated that Kosevo Brigade has mortar positions (including 120-millimetre mortar) in the Mrkovici area. These positions have not been visited by UN personnel in at least four months ..." [Interpretation] And bullet 5 says: [In English] "Shoot reps from the BSA Kosevo Brigade." [Interpretation] Can we go to the following page. There were no reports about the shooting from the Kosevo Brigade of the Serb army. The Kosevo Brigade area -- [In English] "-- on 5th of February. The explosion in the market was recorded as an incoming round from UNMOs on the BH side, but with no indication of the origin of fire." [Interpretation] In the conclusion, it says: [In English] "... mortars easy to hide and equally easy to move. From Appendix 1, it can be seen that the Serb position at Mrkovici is the nearest known position to the directional bracket. However, there could be any number of well-concealed 120-millimetre mortar positions which are unknown to UNPROFOR personnel on either side of the confrontation line within the estimated range bracket. It can only be concluded from this assessment that, in theory, the fire could have originated from either side of the confrontation line." [Interpretation] The first investigation says it was the Muslims, the second investigation says it could be both, and the investigation that you are referring to, General, what is your comment?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you've been reading is a series of technical assessments from a technical document. I don't have any technical knowledge of the subject. I can only say what I've already said and repeat myself: My view at the time was that it was most likely fired from the Bosnian Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you're basing that on what? Give us some grounds. Here, we can see the investigation that you're referring to, and the results are different. The first investigation results that you communicated to the Muslim officers that gave them a fright was that it was their fault. The second investigation was inclusive. Now, what makes you say that it was the Serbs? What do you base that on?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking me to try and recall the various elements which led to my statement to the press at the time. That was some 15 years ago. I have no memory of what those elements were; partly made up from technical reports, no doubt, partly my own observations of what had happened at Dobrinja two days before. That was my position then, that is my position now. It was most likely fired by the Serb side, with regards to the bomb in the Markale market-place. I can add no more to the discussion than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before moving further, Ms. Edgerton, I note this is a document of 64 pages, but do you agree that this part at page 42 in e-court is the conclusionary part of the second investigation, so to speak?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Not immediately, because I've seen another paragraph titled the same way. If I could find that and have a look, I could advise you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I saw the same formulation in page 60, yes. Please move on, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir -- General, sir, please understand me. Not only was a general convicted to a lifetime prison sentence for this, but also there cannot be a reconciliation it was us who fired at Markale, and we didn't. I say so. Look at page 48. And while we're waiting for that page to be produced, do you agree that apart from the technical means and radars, there's no other means or ways to establish the origin of that shell? Am I right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only way of establishing the location of a firing point beyond all reasonable doubt is either from direct observation by the UN Military Observers, which was not the case, or by mortar radar, which we didn't have at the time, so the conclusions from crater analysis will never be technically 100 per cent accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now let's see what the general conclusion says: [In English] "It is to be noticed that during the whole meeting, Bosnian declarations were aggressive at UNPROFOR general policy, blaming for its incompetence and lack of abilities of its members and accusing at several times that UN or UNPROFOR members often stated on Bosnian responsibility in the market shelling." [Interpretation] The general conclusion was that they were rather nervous, and we can also see that on several occasions representatives of UN and UNPROFOR stated Muslim Bosnian responsibility for the shelling of their own people, and after that, everything was done -- all different means were used in order to ascribe the incident to Serbs. Were you familiar with this conclusion, General?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, just before there's an answer on that: With respect to your query to me, the general conclusions to this report are found at e-court page 10, actually -- page 11, pardon me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: General conclusion of ...?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: This second technical analysis. That's what I understood your question to be, Your Honour. And these documents we've been going back to, I note, with the same questions over and over and over again are derived from annexes to that report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You refer to this page, what we are seeing now?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let's look at page 11. Can we please produce page 11 in e-court. It's already there. Okay, very well. Let's look at the findings: [In English] "Time and location of the explosion. Based on witness testimony, it can be concluded that the explosion occurred between 1210 and 1215 hours on 5th of February, 1994 ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We all can read the document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I'd like to point out is the fact that the witness said that the empty market was overcrowded. We saw in the clip that there were no guards, and there's no chance that there were so many people there, but let's look at the bottom of the page, where it says "Culpability." [In English] "There is sufficient physical evidence to prove that one party or the other fired the mortar bomb. The mortar bomb in question could have been fired by either side."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Move on to your next question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have we completed the subject of Markale? If the Trial Chamber understands not only that it was established beyond any reasonable doubt that it was not the Serbs but the Muslims, it's very important and it's very important for the reconciliation. If you want to look at the diametre of the crater, once again, we have UN reports about the crater. Maybe, before we move on, maybe we could look at page 26. Page 26, please, and then 27. Page 26 in e-court, please. This is an analysis, Jose Grande [phoen]: [In English] "On 10th February 1994, I was instructed ..." And so on and so forth. [Interpretation] He analysed and he established that the weapon was a 120-millimetre mortar: [In English] "... gave bearing of the firing position, 420 mils and possible range 800 to 5.000 metres." [Interpretation] Can we go to the following page. Let's look where it says "Possible Range," and let's look at the second paragraph, where he says: [In English] "... had been excavating and slightly enlarged that have been inspected by the previous analysis team."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This means that after the second analysis, General, which pointed to the Muslim origin of the fire, between the first and the second analysis somebody had been excavating, digging, and enlarged the crater; ever so slightly, however. Does this not point to the fact that the first investigation and results were more accurate?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already given you my view of events, and I can add nothing more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let's see what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I remember you were on page 48 before we moved on to page 11.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Edgerton called up page 11, so I wanted to help her with that. And now we will hopefully see 48. Oh, we've already done 48. I don't have anything to show from this document. I believe that the entire document has been admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You didn't ask a question about page 48 after reading out some passage. What was your question? Then if you don't need to ask a question, we can move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked the general whether he was familiar with this conclusion. That's what I asked the general.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember the conclusion of the second report, saying that it could have come from either side. But as I've said already, come to the conclusion that it was most likely to have come from the Serb side -- and I've already made a statement to the media to that effect, and I've given you my reasons, as best I recall them, for having made that statement to the press. I can add nothing further to the discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So how did I conclude that it was from the Serbian side? It was totally excluded from the first investigation, and in the second investigation there was a reasonable -- there was reasonable doubt or, rather, there was no conclusive conclusion, or maybe the interpretation I'm receiving is wrong. General, we have the analysis here. What is the grounds for you persisting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That is asked and answered several times. Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. He's -- Dr. Karadzic is arguing with General Rose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Quite true. Move on to your next topic, Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. 1D2448 is the next document I would like to call. 1D02448, yes, that's the document. And can we look at page 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, do you agree that this was issued on the 7th of February, 1994, and that this is a UN report; right? I would like to draw your attention to the first lines of the Monday chapter: [In English] "The media reported General Rose's statement that it was not known who fired, as the shell had first hit some stalls and changed its trajectory." [Interpretation] So you knew more then than you do now; right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure which this newspaper report is referring to, in terms of statements I made. If it's my major statement to the press about the market-place bombing, then it is an incomplete report of my statement, because I went on to say that it was not possible to say, particularly, specifically who had fired the bomb, but in my opinion it was most likely to have been fired by the Serbs because of the events two days before at the Dobrinja bread queue and UN aid queue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a UN report dated 7 February. This report conveys the way you were quoted by the media. I can't be more precise than that. Could this document be admitted, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll admit this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D682, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D02446, please, could I have that now. We don't have a translation here, regrettably. This is a transcript of the MUP. It was the Muslim police that recorded General Ramsey's conversation with General Milovanovic. Yes, that's it, that's it. May I read a portion of it. It says: "The MUP of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the State Security Service," and so on and so forth, "on the 5th of February, 1994." So that is that very day. It's around 1500 hours. General Ramsey called General Milovanovic because he had been told that Milovanovic had wanted to speak to him. Milovanovic wanted to talk to General Rose, but Ramsey responded that Rose is in Mostar, and he offered to speak to him, himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you in Mostar on that day, General?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in Mostar on the day of the bombing of the market-place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Milovanovic then conveyed a message for General Rose orally, and it says here: "On the basis of an awareness that the Muslim side had accused the Army of Republika Srpska for activities within the inner part of Sarajevo," that is to say, the city, itself, "today, at around 1220 hours, an incident occurred that resulted in a large number of casualties." And then it says further on: "With the intention of establishing all the relevant facts and establishing the truth, this is what I request: that a mixed military commission be established consisting of representatives of UNPROFOR, representatives of the VRS, and the so-called ARBiH, that would prepare a report by tomorrow morning at 8.00, at the latest, and which would investigate all the circumstances that led to this unfortunate incident. That means that this investigation would be completed by tomorrow morning at 8.00 a.m. The work of the mixed military group has to be documented, which includes recording, using cameras, TV cameras, and the like." Tell us, General, was this conveyed to you, this request of General Milovanovic's, to establish a mixed military commission for this investigation?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall, but it may have been, should have been. And I would have certainly forwarded it, in that case, to Mr. Akashi in Zagreb, who I know had already started to assemble an investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember why Serb participation was not accepted, or, rather, this joint commission?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Number 3 says: "Once the professional mixed military team completes its task, the international public should be made aware of the result, regardless of whose fault the incident is." That is paragraph 3 of General Milovanovic's request. Can we now have the next page, please. See this here? General Ramsey says: "All right. That case is going to be investigated in detail. As always, it will be done by UNPROFOR." And then Milovanovic, M, says: "But not in the way in which the Dobrinja case was investigated. I do not acknowledge or accept the investigation that was carried out in that way. Why is Mr. Ramsey avoiding the establishment of a joint commission?" He's saying this in the third person because they're speaking through an interpreter. And General Ramsey says: "Because I cannot guarantee security in the case of such an incident." Do you know that the Serb side challenged the findings in Dobrinja? That is what Milovanovic is saying to Ramsey.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may have known at the time -- I may have known at the time, but I certainly can't recall it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us go on. Milovanovic says: "The only thing that I'm asking you to do is to establish a mixed commission consisting of representatives of the warring parties under UNPROFOR protection." And Ramsey says: "General, I suggest that you be a member of that commission." Milovanovic says: "Yes, if General Ramsey is a member of the commission, himself." And so on and so forth. So, General, from the first moment onwards, the Serb side is clearly stating that they request an investigation. They want proper insight and they want to participate in the investigation. Was the Serb side allowed to do that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
