utterances.text: Well, certainly the team that was formed did not include the Serb side, and I have no memory or recall as to why that was the case. The team was put together - second team, I'm talking about - in Zagreb by Mr. Akashi. Why it was decided there should not be a representative from the Bosnian Serb side, I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You know that the local police did something or the other over there as well, so one warring party was enabled to do this and the other one was not; right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Bosnian Government forces, of course, were on site at the time, and they were able, I think, to carry out an investigation of their own, as the French investigation team derived. They were second on the scene. So the first people on the scene were the Bosnian state authorities, the second on the scene were the French UN team.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With all due respect, the Bosnian authorities had already been there. The explosives experts had already been there, and we have that on film. Can this be admitted; marked for identification, that is?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have any observation in marking this for identification, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I take it Dr. Karadzic is asserting that this intercept, prepared by the Bosnian authorities, is authentic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it he is.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: On that basis, I'd simply request it be translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll mark it for identification, pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D683.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Just for the sake of clarification, we are challenging the legality and legitimacy of peace time intercepts, when our partners in government had no right to wire-tap our communications, whereas this is an intercept of two different parties. Could we now have 65 ter --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note it was too fast.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In addition to that, the intercept, itself, has been corroborated by all the other documents. The 65 ter number is 19612.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, do you remember that the chief of staff - in the translation, there is no name, but it's probably a brigadier general - that he sent you a letter on the 5th of February, 1994, and it was addressed to you personally? It was sent to Kiseljak. 19612 is the 65 ter number, or actually it's 686, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is in evidence as Exhibit P1652, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this technical time not be taken away from my very own time?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember this letter that General Milovanovic sent to you? In the Serbian version, it is one page, and in English it is two pages. On the same day, Milovanovic asks, in writing, the same thing that he asked General Rasek [phoen] to do, or, rather, Ramsey over the telephone. Please cast a glance at this letter and tell us whether it was delivered to you. It says up here that it was received.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly don't remember the letter, receiving it, but it looks entirely possible that I should have or would have done. Can we see the second page of it, please, on the English version?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the second page in English, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it's General Milovanovic asking, in five paragraphs, for the same thing that we had already heard him asking from General Ramsey over the telephone. Can this document be admitted? Thank you, it has been admitted already. Is this the time for the break or should I go on? Should I move on to a new topic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We have about 20 minutes more before the second break.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, we both remember the Gorazde crisis full well, don't we?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: We do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I have to say, for the record, that the learned Ms. Edgerton, as she explained why this material of yours should be kept, she said that I mentioned the third strategic objective, that the Drina should not be a border between Serbs. I have to repeat all the time that Drina should not be a border between two worlds, the East and the West, and that is exactly what the record of the Assembly says. And I don't admit to anything else. Now we are opening the subject of Gorazde. General, do you remember that you were exerting considerable pressure at me to allow eight of your observers to enter Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you recall that I relented and that they, indeed, came to Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did I make a mistake, General?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be for -- up to you to decide, but I think visibility was no bad thing from both points of view, as to what was happening on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now you're going to see that I did, indeed, make a mistake. 1D -- actually, 1D -- oh, it's already been admitted. D137, that's it. We shouldn't be confused by the date. This is a retrospective analysis of Joint Operations Centre of Land Operations in Zagreb. We just have it in the English. That's the document, yes. So although the date is 1995, this is a retrospective analysis. Can we have page 6 of this document, please. At the time, General Janvier was the commander; right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea. I was out of the country by then. I had not been in the country for six months, and I don't know when he handed over -- when General De Lapresle, who was my military boss in Zagreb, handed over to General Janvier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. May I draw your attention to this paragraph: "The B and H will continue ..." [In English] " ... to try to block DutchBat in their OPs or in positions in front of the B and H. This will involve the use of force. They can co-locate within UN positions to use them as human shields. This might provoke a reaction from the Bosnian Serb Army, with a risk for UN personnel to get caught in cross-fire between both factions. The BH is likely to attempt to capture weapons and vehicles from DutchBat to compensate for their lack of armament." [Interpretation] Do you remember that the Muslim side actually drew your observers in near Gorazde, and that is where they were caught in this cross-fire?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see the connection between a document written a year and a half later -- or a year and a quarter later, to what we're discussing at Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, this is what the link is: It's the pattern. First of all, the Muslim side counted on arms smuggling, but it also counted on seizing weapons from the UN forces. That can be seen from this official paragraph of the UN analysis. Don't you see why the Serb side said that you should not bring weapons into the enclaves, weapons that you did not need? First of all, do you see that quite evidently from this portion?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot comment on anything that happened outside my tour of duty in Bosnia. But during my time in Bosnia, the only people that took weapons from the UN, to the best of my knowledge, were the Serbs. The Bosnian state forces did not take weapons from the UN forces during my time, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You will see that that was the case. But I'm going to ask you, here and now, about getting the UN in as a human shield and getting them caught up in cross-fire. That is one thing. And the other thing was the danger that the UN was aware of; namely, that the Muslim side could seize weapons from them. Let us skip one paragraph and move on to the next one: [In English] "Similar to what happened in Gorazde spring 1994, the BiH can attempt to draw UNPROFOR, including the rapid reaction forces or NATO, into the conflict on BH side. Sudden abandoning of positions along the confrontation line, the simulation of a collapse of the enclave or alarming reports from Bosnian side on the situation in the enclaves will be indicators for this. A stronger involvement of the international community could be interpreted by the BSA as an incentive to step up operations and try to eliminate the enclave, as well as retaliate against UN forces." [Interpretation] This is a UN document, General, and you were a UN commander. The reference here is to the situation in Gorazde while you were commander. We're trying to establish a pattern here, the pattern of behaviour of the Muslim side. And the UN was aware of that pattern.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: We certainly formed a view, in 1994, during the events in Gorazde, that the forces there tried to draw NATO in further to the conflict by withdrawing their forces from their defensive positions in order to require greater assistance from NATO air support. And on one occasion, certainly, we saw them move back, which left our observers exposed, and it was during that period that we had one observer killed and one injured. It's an event which we discussed yesterday. Now, whether that was a result of deliberate policy or whether that was a result of a military decision brought about by the pressure your forces were bringing to bear on the Muslims, it is difficult to say, but we certainly formed the impression that they were trying to involve NATO in their war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This has already been admitted, this document, I mean, and it shows that your highest ranking command in Yugoslavia believes that this is a pattern of behaviour of the Muslim side. 1D2509, could we have that document now, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, refrain from making comments, which is not helpful at all.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just agreed with the general. Can we have 1D2509.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, you also do remember - you were a participant and a witness - that the games around Gorazde were massive and aimed at accusing the Serbs. Do you recall that in addition to this abrupt withdrawal, leaving your people at these forward positions, there was also propaganda involved with regard to the level of destruction, the number of fatalities, and so on?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This is an analysis of a team on terrorism and unconventional warfare. It's from the US Congress, and it's in the club of Republican representatives in the US Congress. Can we scroll down so that we can see all of this paragraph that starts with: "The roots ...," et cetera. It's May 1994, so it's right after the crisis in Gorazde; right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, this commission says: [In English] "The roots of this situation derived from the events of the fall of 1992, at a relatively early stage of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. At that time, the Gorazde area was one of the first places where Islamist guerrillas - a combined force of Afghan volunteers (mainly Arab Afghans) and Bosnian Islamists - had embarked on a systematic campaign against the local Christian population in order to secure a predominant military position." [Interpretation] You were aware of the fact that the Muslim Army had expelled Serbs, and killed quite a few, at that, and they burned their houses in and around Gorazde. You saw the houses, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm not going to read all of it: [In English] "The growing frequency of these ambushes, many committed against Serb civilians, made them a dominant feature of the civil war in Bosnia and Herzegovina." [Interpretation] So it's not that these Serbs in the surrounding villages were victims before, but they continued to be victims. Do you know that very often the Muslims left town and went on a rampage around these villages?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you know, we had very limited observation in Gorazde prior to the deployment of the JCOs, to which we've already referred, and, therefore, we did not receive reports. And before the attack on Gorazde, there had been a repetition of what had happened in 1992 and 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You're referring to Muslim attacks against Serbs; right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, one point: It would be helpful to know the origin of the document that is on the screen, to which my attention has been drawn. I can see a letterhead at the top, but not much more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can you see the bottom of the page?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can see the bottom, and now I can see the top as well, sir. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is the US Congress, House Republican Research Committee in the Congress of the United States. That is to say, it's the Republican Party. It is their research committee. And we see here who the heads of that committee are. Does that satisfy your curiosity?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page: [In English] "It was at this point in early 1993 that the Bosnian Muslims began rebuilding Gorazde as a military centre." [Interpretation] Let me not read the entire passage. I'm kindly asking the participants to read it for themselves, and that includes you, General, sir. You will see how things transpired immediately before your arrival in Bosnia. And then after everybody has read that, we will invite your comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see the sentence in which it says that that was possible: [In English] "This was possible because UNHCR demanded that the Bosnian Serb forces withdraw from the immediate road between Sarajevo and Gorazde in order to assure that there would be no interference with its humanitarian work. Consequently, the flow of Bosnian Muslim military supplies increased to the point that, by the end of April 1993, the Muslim forces had effectively relieved the siege of Gorazde." [Interpretation] Do you see that this commission found that the removal of the siege of Gorazde did not improve the humanitarian situation, but, rather, to the increase of the military power of the military force in Gorazde; am I right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I really can't comment on anything that happened prior to my period of command. This is referring to something that happened -- events that may or may not have happened in 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we then go to the next page. And that was already at the time when you were there. The following page in the same document, please. It says: [In English] "Also on 6th of April, the double character of Sarajevo depiction of events in Gorazde became clear. On one hand side, it was presenting an impression to the Western media that a near defenceless Gorazde, full of civilians and innocents, was on the brink of collapse. On the other hand, the government propaganda depicted for domestic consumption a case of heroic and successful combat by the Muslim troops defending Gorazde against a Serb offensive." [Interpretation] And then somewhat lower: [In English] "... meeting the collapse of certain defence lines, Sarajevo, nevertheless stressed that the Muslim defendants were inflicting heavy losses on the Serbs." [Interpretation] And then further on it says that the propaganda in Sarajevo demanded explicitly from the West to intervene and to provoke the United States of America, NATO, and the UN to intervene.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with all that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very much in line with the position I've already taken. And what I read here reflects very much my memory of the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now you will see how wrong I was to accept your pressures and allow the eight observers to enter. It says here: [In English] "... intervention because it already knew that the US, UNPROFOR, and NATO had decided to create in Gorazde circumstances admitting NATO air-strikes within a confine of the existing UN resolution and guide-lines. Thus, on April 7 the UN deployed eight soldiers to Gorazde in order to give itself a legal pretext for its planned air-strikes." [Interpretation] Further on, it says -- or, rather, quotes the resolutions: [In English] "... the UN belonged to the British elite SAS who were qualified and specially equipped to call in and direct air-strikes. In other words, UNPROFOR deployed at one stroke both the excuse and the means to deliver air-strikes against Bosnian Serbs."

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would absolutely deny that there was any predetermination or intention UNPROFOR or any member of the United Nations to create in Gorazde circumstances permitting NATO air-strikes. That is just not the case. The fact that the JCOs were sent there was a result not of a wish to call air-strikes, but to get greater visibility on the ground as to what was happening, the resident UNMO proving not to be as reliable as we had hoped in his reporting. There was no intention to create a situation there, from the UN perspective, where it would be inevitable that air-strikes would happen. That was the decision of last resort, as far as we were concerned, if we decided that the enclave was under sufficiently heavy attack from the Bosnian Serbs. It was not a predetermination to do that, come what may, and as a result of the pressure that the Bosnian Serbs began to bring to bear on the civilian community in Gorazde. Now, what -- whether the US or NATO had predetermined something, you would have to ask them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it, therefore, possible that behind your back NATO had planned and misused you, who talked me into allowing the JCOs to enter to help the SAS? It was not the UN, but it may have been NATO?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you're sure that NATO did not plan it either, or you don't know what they planned. You said a while ago that you don't know what the United States and NATO had in plan, what did they preconceive.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, but I do know the decision to deploy the JCOs was entirely my decision and my decision only. I was under no pressure from anyone. In fact, I doubt if the US or NATO even knew that we had decided to deploy JCOs to Gorazde. It was a UN matter, nothing to do with NATO or the United States. [Overlapping speakers]. The fact that we had to call air-strikes, I'm afraid, was a consequence of your actions, not of NATO's.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We will see that in the course of your cross-examination. However, do you agree with me -- are we coming to the next break, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This is the time. If it is convenient, we will have a break for 25 minutes, resuming at quarter to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We left it off with JCOs. Allow me to say that I am not saying that you were aware about those back-hand games by NATO and others. When it comes to the eight soldiers that I allowed to enter Gorazde, were they all forward air controllers?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The soldiers that were deployed to Gorazde were military observers. They had the ability to call in air-strikes if the need arose. They were certainly not all forward air controllers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did they report correctly about what they had observed and what they attended?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On the other hand, in your statement dated 13 January 2009, when you spoke about UNMOs that you were not responsible for, right, you state this: [In English] "... inaccurate reporting from Gorazde. I told him that misleading reports had done great damage to the credibility of the United Nations mission." [Interpretation] Is that so?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can you identify the para number, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 103, the statement dated 13 January 2009, page number 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: UNMOs, the ones in question, were not the ones who you introduced to Gorazde, the eight men that were deployed in Gorazde; right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. The UNMOs referred to here were the resident UNMOs who were, as I suggested in this statement, misreporting, gave a false impression as to the realities on the ground, and that did not help the UN position.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that all those reports that they sent were damaging to the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly didn't read all their reports verbatim, but the ones I did read exaggerated the damage that was being done by the Serb side with regards to the buildings in Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we see the following page of the same document that is now in e-court. I would like to draw everybody's attention to the paragraph which starts with the words: [In English] "The Bosnian Serb forces advancing from the east were finally able to reach and seize a strategic plateau overlooking Gorazde called Mount Gradina. Although there are easy approach routes from there into Gorazde, the Bosnian Serbs did not show any inclination to continue into the city itself."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That was your assessment also. You believed that the Serbs had no intention to take Gorazde itself; right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, that was, indeed, my conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Obviously, this text also says -- later on you continued to believe the same. We have a document that we are going to show, but let's take another look at the page to see -- [In English] " ... Bosnian Serb positions, instigating a Bosnian Serb shelling. This incident was depicted by the Western media in Sarajevo as an example --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused please indicate the portion he's reading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, the interpreters couldn't follow you. Could you indicate what part you are reading from?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: This is the part that starts: "On 9th of April ...," and in the middle of this: "This was depicted --" I think cursor is showing: "Indeed, special attention was paid to the frequent fire aimed at the hospital - which was also the main Muslim observation and battle management post - to drum up support for Western actions against the Serbs. Subsequently, the UN and NATO were asked to launch air-strikes in order to protect the UN troops that had been inserted into Gorazde." [Interpretation] And then the following paragraph says that on the 10th of April, the Bosnian Serb forces continued to advance slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree, General, that this report suggests that NATO was invited as close-air support to save the United Nations and not to attack the Serbs because they had attacked Gorazde? Close-air support is a legitimate thing, something that we accepted; right?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I don't see how General Rose can be asked to comment on a document that is as thick as this one, that he has only -- he's not had an opportunity to see in full, and he's only been asked questions about specific passages. In fact, General Rose has been at pains, at one point in time, to refute passages of this document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't agree that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. Karadzic. What was your last question, whether the general would agree that this report suggested NATO is invited as close-air support to save the United Nations? Can you answer the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can, sir. Whatever the report may or may not allege, the grounds for calling in close-air support was not to protect the UN personnel there; it was to deter further attacks against the civilian population of Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The general fully understands what I'm on about because we were there at the same place, both of us, and Ms. Edgerton obviously does not share that knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "Close-air support" means support for UN troops which are in danger; right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Close-air support" is a technical term for the capability of the aircraft of a specific sort. It is not air defence. Close-air support is support given by specially-equipped aircraft to troops on the ground or, in this case, to support the UN mission in its efforts to deter further attacks against the civilian population. Close-air support is designed to attack tanks, artillery, and other military installations on the ground. It is a technical expression, without any political connotation at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But, General, sir, there is a difference between two aspects of air support. One is close-air support to help UN troops under attack, and the second is involvement in war developments, with a view to changing the situation in the theatre of war. In other words, that attack in Gorazde was not to assist UN troops but, rather, to alter the situation on the ground and to influence the developments on the ground; right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you have to differentiate between a technical capability and the purpose for which it is used. Certainly, the United Nations limited the use of close-air support on this occasion to deterring attacks against the civilian population of Gorazde. There may or may not have been elsewhere a desire to raise that level of attack and go for more strategic or operational-level targets for political reasons, but that was something which I have no knowledge of and which we would not have accepted, had that been suggested to us, that we go to another level of attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that you, Mr. Akashi, and other officers literally begged them not to try and involve you into that war on the side of any of the warring parties, right, and that you claimed that any operative or strategic involvement or air-strikes would make you -- or, rather, turn you into one of the warring parties? We could read that in your statements, in your telegrams, in your letters; right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was certainly a debate at a higher level between NATO and the United Nations as to whether NATO support should be widened to bring political pressure on the Bosnian Serb side. It was something the United Nations rejected as a possible way ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now look at this same page, which needs to be scrolled down: [In English] "It was at this point that UNPROFOR arranged for another cease-fire on April 11th. At first, the Bosnian Serb artillery honoured the cease-fire, and UNPROFOR acknowledged that the Bosnian Serbs were holding their fire. However, soon afterwards ..." [Interpretation] Scroll down a little, please, for the benefit of the interpreters. Oh, well, we have to go to the next page. The next page, please. It has to be the next page. The next page in English, yes. We see: "On the 11th of April ...," where the cursor is at the moment. [In English] "However, soon afterwards several Muslim raids were finally answered by the Bosnian Serbs. A clash ensued and quickly escalated into a fire-fight that included the use of artillery and mortars on both sides." [Interpretation] Then a further bit down, it says: [In English] "... mortar fire from inside Gorazde." [Interpretation] And now at the very bottom of the page: [In English] "The UN ground commander asked the Muslims 'to stop their provocations in Gorazde.'"

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you agree with this, and do you remember that you stated this?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember making that request.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It says here: [In English] "Indeed, in an interview with French TV TF1, on April 12th General Rose acknowledged ..." Next page in English, please. "... that the Muslims 'shoot on the Serbs to step up the pressure and obtain a fresh intervention from NATO.'" [Interpretation] Did you state that for the French television?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember whether I stated that or not to the French television, but we've already agreed that it was a general policy of the Bosnian Government to try and draw NATO forces in to help them in their war against the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May I draw attention to the middle of the following paragraph. Let me invite everybody to read this. And it says that they concentrated their weapons around the Red Cross building, which was marked. And from there, they opened fire against the Bosnian Serbs, and the Bosnian Serb forces were advancing towards the banks of the Drina River. Infantry fighting -- [In English] "-- and clashes soon expanded along the entire front-line east of Gorazde. Needless to say, it did not take long for the Bosnian Serbs to react to this action." [Interpretation] Do you remember that the Muslims employed that tactic, that they deployed their weapons around the hospital and the Red Cross facility, and from there they opened fire on the Serbs? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that at all. I wasn't there. You say you were there. I was where I should have been, which was in my headquarters in Sarajevo, at the operational level of command. I was not at the tactical level forward. We only had, as I pointed out, some observers there, be it from the JCO and from the United Nations Military Observer unit. If it's any reassurance to you, I visited shortly afterwards and found that the hospital, if that's the building you're referring to, had only been hit by one shell which had hit right up on the top and, according to the doctor at the time, hadn't caused any casualties. Of course, if you had been aiming at it continuously, then there may be some lack of reassurance to you in terms of the accuracy of your own artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Or perhaps we didn't want to target the hospital. Would that be a possible explanation, General?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would have been an explanation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can I draw everybody's attention to this: We can see that this is Muslim propaganda in action at the end of the paragraph, "Before the 15th of April ..." that's one part of the tactic. And can we now go to the following page. It says here: "In mid-April ..." [In English] "In mid-April, with Gorazde seemingly on the verge of collapsing, NATO air operations and related military activities intensified. The British SAS team significantly expanded the zone of the infiltration activities in order to identify, locate, and mark Bosnian Serb targets for subsequent air attack." [Interpretation] And it says that one of the SAS troops was killed and another wounded in the ensuing fire-fight. And at the end of the paragraph, you can read: [In English] "Meanwhile, UN observers were randomly deployed in forward Bosnian Muslim positions, at times only 500 metres from the front-line, without any advance warning to the Bosnian Serb side. Consequently, UNPROFOR personnel would suddenly appear in the Bosnian Muslim position in the middle of the fire-fight, demanding that Bosnian Serbs hold their fire or else risk NATO air-strikes."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then they withdrew suddenly and left you people out in the cold; right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already said, the JCO observers were positioning themselves to get best visibility of what was happening on the ground, and at one point they got caught, after the Bosnian Government forces withdrew, in a cross-fire between the Bosnian Government forces and the Bosnian Serb forces, and, tragically, one of them was killed and another injured. I've already explained that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we go to the next page, please, where it says: "The 17th of April ..." We can see that the Bosnian Serbs withdrew their main tanks and guns to a distance of three kilometres on the 17th of April, and the Bosnian Muslim forces exploited the absence of the heavy guns and opened fire on the Bosnian Serb positions." And further on it says: [In English] "With the Bosnian Muslims complaining on the ammunition shortage, the Bosnian Serbs insisted on thorough inspection of all the humanitarian convoys because they were allowed to go to Gorazde through Bosnian Serb lines. Considering that the UN had been instrumental in building the Bosnian Muslim forces in Gorazde, it was not an illogical demand." [Interpretation] And further on it says: "On the 18th of April ..." [In English] "... Karadzic promised to implement yet another unilateral cease-fire and withdrew some of his heavy weapons three kilometres away from the outskirts of Gorazde as the first phase of a regional cease-fire. Once again, soon after the Bosnian Serbs withdrawal began, the Bosnian Muslims forces opened fire on the Bosnian Serb positions, and again the Bosnian Serbs turned around and resumed their shelling. On the 18th of April, the Bosnian Muslims established a new long-range fire position ..." [Interpretation] And so on and so forth. And: [In English] "Indeed, the UN was still using the fifth floor facility while the Bosnian Muslims fortified the third and fourth floor." [Interpretation] So they are nicely leading us to NATO aircraft, and we have no way of avoiding that. As soon as we turn our backs, they start firing at us. General, did you ever see anyone wage warfare under such difficult conditions like the Serbs? The entire world is against us, and also there are cheap tricks being played by the Muslims, and NATO accepts that and firmly stands on their side.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I make no comment on that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Could we have the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then came the bombing; right, General? The bombing started on the 10th, and you very chivalrously accepted that you had called those aircraft in and that they bombed the Serbs; right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us see what your men were doing. Let us look at page 114 of the book. I beg your pardon. Yes, yes, you're right, it's 1D1 -- 1D10137 [as interpreted]. For the moment, we have to get rid of this document, and then we'll have it called back after a while, but now let's look at General Rose's book. It is page 114 in the book, itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 1D1037, the general's book, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would like to draw your attention to your own words: [In English] "On the fourth pass over Gorazde, the lone Sea Harrier was shut down. The incident happened within sight of a forward air controller who was at the time talking to the headquarter in Sarajevo. Suddenly we heard him saying, 'A 21 Fortune 5 is tracking a tank along the road. We now have communications with the aircraft, and we are directing it on the tank. The aircraft now can see the tank. He got -- he's got it visual. The aircraft has been hit and is on fire. It's going down. I think the pilot has ejected. I can see a parachute.'" [Interpretation] Could you please explain to the Trial Chamber what a forward air controller is.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: A forward air controller is somebody who is trained to call in air-strikes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does he target?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is his specific role, to target enemy objectives on the ground, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it done by a laser or what?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The technical capabilities have changed much over the years.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So if there are two who are taking part in the firing, if there is one gunner and -- if there is one in the aircraft and the other one on the ground, there is two of them; right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: A forward air controller would not be firing at a target, himself, when calling in aircraft.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Probably what I said was misinterpreted. If there are two who are firing, there is one who is setting the sights, the one on the ground, the one that I allowed into Gorazde, and the one who is actually firing is the one in the aircraft; right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The one on the ground is targeting the aircraft, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Don't you think that that turns him into a combatant?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends on the level of force used. In this case, it most certainly did not turn the UN into one of the combatants. He was merely being used in support of the resolution which called on us to deter all attacks against the safe area using all means possible. Had the United Nations accepted a higher level of force and agreed to strategic-level targets, then there may be an argument for stating that. But it is not the case, during 1994, that we ever went down that route.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, with all due respect, as for the young men who were in the tank and who were hit, that was 100 per cent use of fire. It wasn't tactical, operative, strategic. It was very specific. For my small army, that was a very significant strike, wasn't it? Didn't you turn these young men into combatants because you called in aircraft, and also, in the process, they were the ones who were setting the sights; right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have to distinguish between a peacekeeper, who's either defending himself or carrying out his role under a United Nations Security Council resolution which has been passed in support of a peacekeeping mission, without a war fighting. The United Nations' actions were those of peacekeepers, not war fighters, and a clear distinction should be made.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I think, General, that at the time you were far more critical of NATO, who had abused you. Let us see what Admiral Leighton Smith said. He gave up on further UNPROFOR and NATO engagement, in view of -- in view of the downing of this aircraft. You should know, General, that it was not easy at all for the Serbs to down friendly aircraft that were directed by NATO to turn into hostile aircraft. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure which paragraph you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On this page here, where you're conveying the transcript of the radio communication with the forward air controller who had targeted our tank. One or two tanks were destroyed, and also an ambulance was destroyed. Then there is a photograph of that vehicle that you kept in your officers. And underneath it, it says "Bravo, NATO." So this was criticism against NATO; right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have a photograph in my office with a sign under it saying "Bravo, NATO."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I think that that was the case. Did you have a photograph of the ambulance that NATO had hit in Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did. There's a copy of it on the back of the book, but it did not have --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- "Bravo, NATO" written on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. But after at least one tank had been hit, and an ambulance, too, the next aircraft had been downed; right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the precise sequence of events, but certainly one Sea Harrier was shot down.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. As for this page, we would like to tender it. Could we now have 1312. That's the 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You know, General, that our relations were chilled on several occasions, especially your relations with my officers, my generals, because our position was that you were free to shoot if anyone opened fire at your soldiers. But if you call NATO in to change the balance of forces on the ground, we believed that you were turning into combatants on one particular side. Do you remember that break in our relations?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that when we went to Geneva for peace discussions, your military side refused to talk to me. That's all I remember. As far as we were concerned, we had done the minimum use of force possible in the circumstances, and that we were continuing in our primary role of attempting to deliver humanitarian aid to the people of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. But they did not speak to you; however, that was not personal. But you simply turned into our enemy. You turned into a combatant against us when you called in air-strikes. Did you become engaged? That's the word. Didn't you become a warring party, as it were?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already explained that we did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, this is a question that's been asked of the general and answered in the most straightforward terms. You're simply repeating it, which is a waste of the limited time that you have.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have a look at this telegram now that was sent to the Secretary-General by Mr. Akashi from Zagreb on the 24th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the second paragraph, he says: "General Rose ..." [In English] "... has met with Dr. Karadzic and stated that the Serbs must withdraw from the area or UNPROFOR will be obliged to resort ..." [Interpretation] And so on. [In English] "Karadzic has stated that we will not attack civilians, but he firmly intends to enter the town to destroy the 5th BH Corps." [Interpretation] The translation is wrong: [In English] "Karadzic stated that he firmly intends to enter the town to destroy 5th BH Corps. It is our military judgement that such action will result in civilian casualties." [Interpretation] And then it says that he and you, General Rose: [In English] "... have also been in contact with Vice-President Ganic --" [Interpretation] And so on. [In English] "Karadzic's principal demand is for a general cease-fire. We are convinced that he will settle for nothing less and that there is a real possibility that the Serbs will pursue 5th BH Corps into the town. The consequence of the action we would be required to take in that event requires your decision. The area strikes will require attacks on a number of air defence systems and fixed installations, as it is not possible to employ aircraft against Serb infantry in a populated area. The advantage of this option is its demonstration of United Nations' resolve. The Serbs will also be seen to have paid some price for violation of safe area and may, if strikes are extensive enough, be deterred from further transgressions. This option transforms UNPROFOR into a combatant and will require withdrawal under adverse conditions." [Interpretation] And so on. So Mr. Akashi says that if Serb positions and installations are bombed, that turns the UN into a warring party; right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which paragraph, precisely, were you referring to in that last question, Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The third line from the bottom: [In English] "... UNPROFOR into a combatant."

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he said if strikes are extensive, which is the point which I was making, he, like I, were reluctant or, in fact, refused to accept a higher level of targeting and was commensurate with peacekeeping. And that -- I think his letter reflects that point of view --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you remember, General, that the 5th Corps had attacked us from the zone of Bihac and had reached almost Bosanski Petrovac? They took 300 kilometres of purely Serb land, purely Serb villages. They killed whoever they found and they torched everything.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly don't remember that being the case. When I arrived in 1994, Bihac was an enclave which was subject to United Nations Security Council resolutions regarding the security of those enclaves, and the sequence of events on the ground which led to the Serb attack into that area in November is something that I have no knowledge of.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, we'll get to that. Can we admit this document? It's a telegram of Mr. Akashi's.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think it has already been admitted as Exhibit P1681.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now have 1D2509 once again, the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We're still dealing with Gorazde a bit. We are going to conclude with Gorazde, and then we are going to move on to Bihac. General, would you agree that out of the six safe protected areas, only two were delimited or, rather, it is only Srebrenica and Zepa that had boundaries that were set between the warring parties?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think Sarajevo would have -- which, of course, was one of the safe areas, had pretty clear boundaries in terms of the line of conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I agree as far as the line of conflict is concerned. However, if you remember, when the safe areas were declared as such, an agreement was reached, stating where the boundary of the area is. That is what your documents -- UN documents also say, that the main problem was that these boundaries had not been established. That is one problem. And then there's this other problem that none of the safe areas had been demilitarised. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is certainly the case that there was no clear boundaries marked around the safe areas, all the safe areas. Secondly, there was no requirement, as we've already discussed, by the Bosnian Government forces to demilitarise those safe areas. That was never a requirement put on them by a United Nations Security Council resolution, for the obvious reason that that was their sovereign territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you. Let us have a look at this, where it says: "The 28th of April ..." We're still dealing with Gorazde: [In English] "The 28th of April, General Rose went on an inspection tour of the Gorazde enclave. He returned full of criticism of the Bosnian Muslims, adding that they had exaggerated the number of wounded and the damage done to the town in the Bosnian Serb offensive in order to instigate NATO's military intervention. General Rose stated, 'The situation was a lot better than I had been led to believe. One can only be pleased at that.'" [Interpretation] And so on and so forth. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we admit this document? [In English] The document Task Force on Terrorism and Unconventional Warfare is from -- [Interpretation] It's from the US Congress.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What part of the US Congress, Mr. Karadzic? I note that it's downloaded from a site which is called "serbianlinksfreehosting.net." And I find --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it was just published there, but this was presented at this Republican -- [In English] "The Task Force of Terrorism and Unconventional Warfare, the House of Republican Research Committee, US House of Representatives." [Interpretation] So it's a Republican committee, a committee of Congressmen. Anybody can publish it now. Wherever you find it, you can use it, you can get it off any web site.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: On this one, Your Honours, I wouldn't agree. I think that this is a document that has absolutely no hallmarks of reliability. It's clearly a partisan document, and General Rose on several occasions has spoken about the extent to which he disagrees with it. And, frankly, I don't think it's added a single thing to the written and oral evidence he's already given, in any case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Speaking for myself, Mr. Karadzic, I'm not sure about the foundation of this document. It says it's an executive summary, but executive summary of what? Who's the author? And anybody can turn in papers to a committee of a party. And it has no reference at all, and so at this moment -- I have to consult with my colleagues, but speaking for myself, I'm not satisfied that --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I respond before that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I respond before you take your decision?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document was sent to the United Nations. The next document we will show will show that Mr. Akashi studied it and stated his views on it. This is a research committee of one political party in Congress. It has to do with the study of conventional warfare. If Ms. Edgerton thinks that we should first study the objectivity of each and every document we deal with, then every one of her documents would have to be rejected before we assess these documents. That would be a court within a court. It is for you to adjudicate, ultimately, what is to be decided. However, we can call a document up, and it will show that this document had been shown to the UN. 1D2508, could we have that for a moment, and then you will see what that says. Also, there are some objections with regard to objectivity, but there are certain things here that have been stated correctly. No doubt about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think we have that document you referred to. So what is your point, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in this telegram, it says: [In English] "As requested at your fax of 25th June 1994, we have reviewed the US House Republican Research Committee report of 4 May 1994 on Gorazde. We find the paper lacks objectivity. "Our remarks are based on the examination of our daily records, and the comments of UNMOs who were in Gorazde at the time." [Interpretation] So Mr. Akashi believes that the UN Military Observers have been accused in an unjustified manner. However, General Rose said, no, it was the reports that were wrong: [In English] "It must, however, be borne in mind that our observers in Gorazde were limited in numbers, unable to range widely through the area, and confined to their shelters as the conflict intensified." [Interpretation] In a word, Mr. Akashi is defending his observers, and he is not challenging the authenticity of the document. Does anyone in this courtroom challenge the authenticity of this document? It is for the Trial Chamber to see what its value is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In order to properly assess and determine the probative value of this document, the Chamber should know the members of this committee, as well as who authored or who did the research in relation to this. So on that basis, we'll mark this document for identification, pending -- we are pending until the Chamber is satisfied with its foundation. We'll give it a number, an MFI D number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D684, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this telegram be admitted, this telegram to Akashi?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D685, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And can we now briefly look at D135 that has been admitted already, D135, about the demilitarisation of protected areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we are waiting, General: Do you agree that it should not have been allowed to the Muslim forces to be inside the protected areas, and to attack the surrounding Serb villages from those protected areas, and be protected while in there?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already explained, these enclaves were sovereign territory of the Bosnian Government, and they had every right to locate their forces there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Excellent. But then they were not protected areas, because the neighbouring village was my sovereign territory, and they launched attacks at it and slaughtered civilians, and you protected them in that criminal activity. Do you agree that they should not have attacked the Serb territories from the protected areas, or do you perhaps think that they could and they should have?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, without agreeing to any of your preamble to that question, I agree that it was unhelpful to the peace process that they -- the Bosnian state forces attacked from those enclaves. That much, I do agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Trial Chamber the meaning of a protected area which is full of troops? The Secretary-General said that those were not protected areas but, rather, armed strongholds, that they were strongholds, armed strongholds belonging to the Muslim Army. How can we reconcile the words of the Secretary-General with the term "protected areas"? What constituted a protected area if that area was full of troops that killed people from within that area?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The concept of a safe area or a sanctuary is as old as war, itself, and it depends on the willingness of both parties to a conflict not to use that safe area for their own military purposes, either attacking into or attacking from within outwards. And it is a matter of regret to the United Nations that the Bosnian state forces did attack from within those safe areas outwards, because it was not helpful to the peace process. That much, I can say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In other words, the status of a protected area is based on the agreement of the warring parties; right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: An agreement had certainly been made before my time, and from what I understood between the Bosnian forces and the Bosnian Serbs in the matter of Srebrenica, at the time when General Morillon was the commander of the UNPROFOR. But the overall United Nations Security Council resolutions which flowed from that agreement were somewhat different in their wording, what it might have been agreed then, and limited the actions of the United Nations to deterring all attacks against, but not using the word "protection" or "defend," because, of course, those are military activities, war-fighting activities which peacekeepers are unable to assume.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We can see here an agreement on demilitarisation made between General Mladic and General Halilovic made on the 8th of May 1993 in the presence of General Morillon. Can we please go to the second page of the same document. Let's look at the first paragraph: [In English] "Every military or paramilitary unit will have either to withdraw from the demilitarised zone or submit/hand over their weapons. Ammunition, mines, explosives, and combat supplies in the demilitarised zones will be handed over/submitted to UNPROFOR. "After submission/hand-over of all weapons, ammunition, mines and combat supplies in the demilitarised zone, the contracting parties will declare that the demilitarisation is complete. "Submitting/hand-over will be completed: "A. In Srebrenica by Monday, 10th of May, 1993, by 17 [sic] hours. "In Zepa, by Wednesday, 12th of May ..." And so on. [Interpretation] Can we see the end of the document, and can we see General Mladic's and General Halilovic's signatures on the last page. Here are the signatures. Do you agree that these are the signatures of all the three generals? Was that the basis for the demilitarisation, and not the sovereignty that all of us shared? We were also sovereign in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Was this the basis for the demilitarisation and the protection of those protected areas?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was obliged to conform to the United Nations Security Council Resolutions 824 and 836, and the wording of those two Security Council resolutions do not reflect what was agreed locally in 1993, before those two resolutions were passed, in any way at all regarding demilitarisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, the International Law of War does recognise the agreements on the demilitarisation of certain zones or agreements on not attacking such zones; right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm no expert on international law.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go back to the first page of the document, please. Article 2: [In English] "On the ground of the demilitarised zone shall be marked by UNPROFOR by means of boards on which is stated in English, Serbian and Bosnian, in Cyrillic ..." And so on and so forth: [In English] "... any military operation is strictly forbidden (Article 60, Protocol 1, Additional to the Geneva Conventions)." [Interpretation] In other words, this arises from the International Law of War and the Geneva Conventions as an integral part thereof. Are you saying, General, that we were not allowed to defend ourselves from attacks coming from the demilitarised zones, and they, in their turn, were allowed to launch those attacks against us? Just say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only reply by saying that I was bound by Security Council Resolutions 824 and 836, and what may have occurred before in 1993 was something which I had no knowledge of. It is certainly the case that the Bosnian Government forces continued -- did not demilitarise and continued to attack outwards in spite of the protests we raised from time to time with them. That is true.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Just a correction in the transcript. We were not allowed to defend ourselves from attacks, and not to launch attacks against the demilitarised zone. Can the Court please produce 1D1408. It's a video-clip, and I'm sure you're going to recognise a young man in it. Can we watch from 1:45:33 to 1:46:43.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: "As he flew by helicopter into Gorazde following the fighting, Rose was asked about US satellite reports that nearly every house in Gorazde was damaged. "Yes, practically every house in Gorazde has been damaged, but most of the damage to Gorazde was done in the fighting that had taken place some two years before, when the Bosnian Government forces drove the Serbs from this town, and there were 12 and a half thousand Serbs at that time living here and they were all driven off. The way to distinguish a house that has been damaged by fighting, where a shell has hit it and a house that's been damaged by ethnic cleansing is if it's got no roof, no doors, no window frames, and nothing in the house at all, and there are burn marks and bullets spread around the walls, that is the house that has been damaged by ethnic cleansing. A house that's been damage by shelling has a shell hole in it and there are still people trying to live in that building with their furniture because they've got nowhere else to go. That's something you can't see from satellites, and of course at that time the international image of what had happened in Gorazde was very different from the reality. What was dangerous was that policies were going to be put together on both sides of the Atlantic about what we should do in Gorazde, but these policies had been put together on totally flawed information."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember this interview, General?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember very well making that interview, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this video-clip be admitted. It already has a number. The title of the clip is "A war that could be avoided," but from 1:45:43 to 1:46:43 is the part or the portion of the video-clip that I would like to have admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It shall be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D686, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And before we break off for the day, can we look at 65 ter 7228. 7228.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we are waiting: General, yesterday you estimated quite rightly that Mladic's remark was in respect of the Herzegovina Corps, and it was on the right bank of the Drina River; right? He said that Muslims should not stay there, because on the right bank of the Drina River the villages were Serb, and you said it rightly yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I fail to understand the question, Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, the document referred to the Herzegovina Corps. In Gorazde, on the right bank of the Drina, there was the Herzegovina Corps, and on the left bank of the Drina River, the corps that was deployed there was the Drina Corps; right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I say, I don't have any knowledge of the military deployments amongst any of the warring parties.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. However, my learned friend Ms. Edgerton showed you a document in which Mladic issued an order to the Herzegovina Corps to liberate the right bank, and that was portrayed as Mladic asking for Muslims to be expelled from Gorazde. And your understanding was about the Serbs on the right bank. It was not ordered to the Drina Corps, but rather to the Herzegovina Corps, because that's how they were deployed. But if you don't know, you don't know. It's not a problem. Can we look at document 7228. That's not a document I wanted. 65 ter 7228. Yes, it could be that, yes. Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this has been admitted as Exhibit P1658.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Even better. Let's look at the first paragraph and the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here, General Major Milovanovic, deputy commander, sends information to the Herzegovina Corps at the Forward Command Post, the Drina Corps, the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, the TG Visegrad, and some other units, and he says: "At the joint meeting of the warring parties and representatives of UNPROFOR, the observers reported that they had informed the UN that the Army of Republika Srpska had to date not fired on the town of Gorazde itself, and that operations were generally occurring at the line of conflict and in the surrounding villages behind the line of conflict. Such a report is advantageous to the Republika Srpska and has prevented unfavorable resolutions being adopted by the Security Council." And the last paragraph reads: "The decision of the supreme commander and the commander of the Main Staff of the army is to continue energetically conducting the planned combat operations, but to avoid opening artillery fire on the town of Gorazde itself at all costs (as has mostly been respected so far) --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We can all read.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question:

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, did you, yourself, arrive at the conclusion that most of the fire, which is what you stated in your reports, was on the separation lines and not on the town of Gorazde itself, although that's how it was reported by the Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not agree to that. There was definitely the -- the main effort of the Bosnian Serb side seemed to be on the right bank of the Drina, but equally there was pressure right 'round the enclave against the enclave by the Bosnian forces. I'm sure that was the situation by the 8th of April, although I cannot be certain. The enclave was under attack from the Bosnian Serb forces, albeit the main effort may have been on the right bank, as you suggest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll now take the adjournment until tomorrow afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one more question, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, if we agree that Serb villages were on the right bank, and as we could see in that video-clip, the Muslims had cleansed them ethnically in 1992, and if Mladic wanted to liberate them, obviously he had to tie up the Muslim forces on the other side. As an officer, you wouldn't allow the Muslims to deploy all of their forces on the right bank. How would you have liberated that bank if you had not deployed your troops everywhere? Do you agree with me that it was a logical military decision?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's a hypothetical question which I cannot answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll resume tomorrow afternoon at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 7th day of October, 2010, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.05 p.m.,
